title: RAW_UNREVIEWED: cummin addition is tied specifically to calculus dispersal, not the base drink's other effects
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_UNSELECTED_NOT_TESTED. In Pliny XXII.29's 1856 Bostock/Riley English layer, a drink of helioscopium is said to expel tapeworm and gravel; the clause then specifically adds cummin for dispersing calculi. The speculative constraint is ingredient-to-effect scope: the additive is attached to one changed claimed result, not freely propagated across the neighboring effects. The source's historical efficacy claim is not independently verified, and no target word is proposed.

source_evidence.quote: There are two species of heliotropium, the tricoccum [note 2598] and the helioscopium, [note 2599] the latter being the taller of the two, though they neither of them exceed half [note 2600] a foot in height. The helioscopium throws out branches from the root, and the seed of it, enclosed in follicules, [note 2601] is gathered at harvest-time. It grows nowhere but in a rich soil, a highly-cultivated one more particularly; the tricoccum, on the other hand, is to be found growing everywhere. I find it stated, that the helioscopium, boiled, is considered an agreeable food, and that taken in milk, it is gently laxative [note 2602] to the bowels; while, again, a decoction of it, taken as a potion, acts as a most effectual purgative. The [page 414] juice of this plant is collected in summer, at the sixth [note 2603] hour of the day; it is usually mixed with wine, which makes [note 2604] it keep all the better. Combined with rose-oil, it alleviates head-ache. The juice extracted from the leaves, combined with salt, removes warts; from which circumstance our people have given this plant the name of “verrucaria,” [note 2605] although, from its various properties, it fully merits a better name. For, taken in wine or hydromel, it is an antidote to the venom of serpents and scorpions, [note 2606] as Apollophanes and Apollodorus state. The leaves, too, employed topically, are a cure for the cerebral affections of infants, known as “siriasis,” [note 2607] as also for convulsions, even when they are epileptic. It is very wholesome, too, to gargle the mouth with a decoction of this plant. Taken in drink, it expels tapeworm and gravel, and, with the addition of cummin, it will disperse calculi. A decoction of the plant with the root, mixed with the leaves and some suet of a he-goat, is applied topically for the cure of gout.

design.falsifier: The source-bound contrast fails if the cumin phrase does not restrict the calculi claim or if it must be attached to all previous effects to make grammatical sense.
